notable: Boston won the Players' League pennant in 1890 and the American Association pennant in 1891 here.
Bobby Lowe hit four home runs in one game here on May 30, 1894.
The Beaneaters used it in 1894 while the South End Grounds were rebuilt.

parks.name: Cramton Bowl
parks.status: Still stands as a football stadium.
notable: Hosted the South's first night football game in 1927.
Montgomery Grey Sox played here in 1932.

parks.name: Crosley Field
parks.status: Demolished starting 1972; commercial buildings and a street now cover the site.
notable: Hosted the Cincinnati Tigers (1937), Buckeyes (1942) and Clowns (1943-45) of the Negro American League.
In 1935 it became the first major-league park to host night games.
Hosted the first major league night game in 1935.

parks.name: Crump Park
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the 1932 Little Rock Grays.

parks.name: Culver Field
parks.status: A Gleason Works plant occupies the site.
notable: A fire destroyed the original park in October 1893; it was rebuilt for 1898.
Right-field bleachers collapsed in May 1906, injuring dozens.

parks.name: Dartmouth Street Grounds
parks.status: Site is now occupied by the Copley Place complex.
notable: Home of the Union Association Boston Reds in 1884.
Dupee Shaw struck out 18 St. Louis Maroons there on July 19, 1884.
Railroad tracks, Dartmouth Street and Huntington Avenue bordered the grounds.

parks.name: Dequindre Park
parks.status: Site on Dequindre Avenue south of Six Mile Road; current use not verified.
notable: Listed as the home site of the 1937 Detroit Stars.
Park name not confirmed; only its location on Dequindre Avenue is recorded.

parks.name: Dexter Park
parks.status: Redeveloped with houses and a supermarket in the late 1950s.
notable: Home of the Brooklyn Royal Giants from 1923 to 1931.
Installed New York City's first permanent baseball lights in 1930.
Located in Woodhaven near the Brooklyn border.

parks.name: Durkee Field
parks.status: Still in use; National Register-listed and holding a small museum.
notable: Opened as Barrs Field and rebuilt in 1936-37 after a fire.
Home of the Jacksonville Red Caps in 1938 and 1941-42.

parks.name: East End Park
parks.status: The Schmidt Recreation Complex, with softball fields, occupies the site.
notable: Home of Kelly's Killers from April 25 to August 13, 1891.
Fans often arrived by steamboat; the park had Ohio River access.
Police arrested players during a Sunday game on May 24, 1891.

parks.name: Eastern Park
parks.status: Commercial and light industrial buildings, including a scrap yard, occupy the Brownsville site.
notable: Home to Brooklyn's NL club 1891-97 and the 1890 Players' League Ward's Wonders.
Hard to reach, it was considered a failure as a home.
The Trolley Dodgers nickname first arose here.

parks.name: Ebbets Field
parks.status: Ebbets Field Apartments, opened in 1962, occupy the site.
notable: Hosted the first Brooklyn night game on June 15, 1938 before 38,748 fans.
Staged the 1949 All-Star Game.
Home of Brooklyn's only World Series title, 1955.

parks.name: Eclipse Park
parks.status: Burned in 1892; a second Eclipse Park was built nearby.
notable: Home of the Louisville Eclipse (1882-84) and Colonels (1885-91) during the American Association years.
A fire on September 27, 1892 destroyed it; the 1893 season began in what remained.
First of three Eclipse Parks, named for the original Eclipse club.

parks.name: Eclipse Park II
parks.status: Commercial buildings stand at the site.
notable: Honus Wagner made his major league debut here on July 19, 1897.
A fire on August 12, 1899, forced the Colonels to play their last month on the road.

parks.name: Eclipse Park (Milwaukee)
parks.status: Interstate 43 and the Marquette Interchange cover the site.
notable: Home of the 1878 Milwaukee Grays, who finished last at 15-45 and folded.
Like later Borchert Field, its site now sits under a highway.

parks.name: Exhibition Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1999; BMO Field and a parking lot occupy the site.
notable: Blue Jays home from 1977 through 1989, when the club moved to SkyDome.
The 1977 home opener was played in snow on a covered field.
The 1985 ALCS Game 7 was played here, won by Kansas City.

parks.name: Exposition Park
parks.status: Interstate 279 and parking lots cover the site; a state historical marker commemorates it.
notable: First NL park to host a World Series game, on October 6, 1903.
Pirates were first to cover the field with a tarp in wet weather, in 1906.
Three successive parks stood here; the third hosted the first modern World Series game in 1903.

parks.name: Exposition Park
parks.status: Former ballpark; later uses not recorded in sources checked.
notable: Hosted the first Kansas-Missouri football game on October 31, 1891.
The Cubs and Cardinals played here October 15, 1892, their only meeting outside either home city until 2023.

parks.name: Federal League Park
parks.status: Demolished in 1917; replaced by railroad freight yards near Victory Field.
notable: Built in 1914 for the Federal League Indianapolis Hoosiers, who left for Newark after one season.
Stood on part of the former Greenlawn cemetery.

parks.name: Forbes Field
parks.status: Partly remembered on the University of Pittsburgh campus; left-center wall segment still stands.
notable: First steel-and-concrete ballpark in the National League.
Bill Mazeroski's 1960 Game 7 home run ended the World Series here.
Used by the Homestead Grays in the late 1920s and 1930s.

parks.name: Forepaugh Park
parks.status: Sold for development and covered with houses by 1895.
notable: Drew a record 17,812 on April 30, 1890, when the Athletics hosted the Boston Reds.
Hosted the Players' League Athletics in 1890 and the American Association Athletics in 1891.
Circus promoters staged shows here, including one with the skeleton of Jumbo the elephant in 1886.

parks.name: Freeport Municipal Stadium
parks.status: Current status not verified.
notable: Listed as a 1936 home of the New York Black Yankees.
Details not found; opening year shown is the season of Negro-league use.

parks.name: General Electric Field
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the 1932 Newark Browns of the East-West League.

parks.name: George M. Steinbrenner Field
parks.status: Still in use as the Yankees' spring home and Tampa Tarpons' ballpark.
notable: Rays' temporary home for all of 2025 after Hurricane Milton damaged Tropicana Field.
Its dimensions copy those of both Yankee Stadiums.
Kameron Misner hit a walk-off homer on March 28, 2025, its first regular-season MLB home run.

parks.name: Giants Park
parks.status: Industrial area now; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the St. Louis Giants in 1920 and 1921, most games.
Bounded by North Broadway and Clarence and Prescott Avenues.
Renamed Metropolitan Park around 1934.

parks.name: Globe Life Park in Arlington
parks.status: Still stands as Choctaw Stadium, used for soccer and football.
parks.architect: David M. Schwarz Architectural Services; HKS (architect of record)
notable: Kenny Rogers pitched a perfect game here in 1994.
Hosted the 1995 All-Star Game and World Series games in 2010 and 2011.

parks.name: Gordon and Koppel Field
parks.status: Now Kiely Park, a public park.
notable: Home of the Kansas City Packers in 1914 and 1915.
Nearby Brush Creek flooding sometimes interrupted games.

parks.name: Greenlee Field
parks.status: The Bedford Dwellings housing project occupies the site.
notable: Black-owned park built for Gus Greenlee's Crawfords in 1932.
Homestead Grays also used it from 1932 to 1937.
Satchel Paige pitched to Josh Gibson at the opening.

parks.name: Griffith Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1965. Howard University Hospital stands on the site.
notable: Mickey Mantle's 1953 homer here popularized the term tape measure home run.
Hosted the 1940 NFL title game, a 73-0 Bears win.
Home to the Senators 1911-1960.

parks.name: Hamilton Field
parks.status: Site of the former Camp Allen on the St. Marys River, north of Camp Allen Park.
notable: Hosted the first National Association game on May 4, 1871, a 2-0 Kekiongas win over Cleveland.
Its covered grandstand, the Grand Dutchess, burned down on November 5, 1871.

parks.name: Hamtramck Stadium
parks.status: Still stands in Veterans Park; renovated and reopened in 2022.
notable: Home of the Detroit Stars in 1930 and the Detroit Wolves in 1932.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2012.
Ty Cobb threw out the first pitch at the 1930 opening.

parks.name: Handlan's Park
parks.status: Part of the Saint Louis University campus; a SABR marker stands there.
notable: Home of the Federal League St. Louis Terriers in 1914-15.
The Negro National League St. Louis Giants played here from 1920 to 1922.

parks.name: Hard Rock Stadium
parks.status: Still stands as the home of the Dolphins and Hurricanes; no longer used for MLB.
notable: Marlins won the 1997 and 2003 World Series here.
Football-first design left poor baseball sightlines and brutal summer heat.
World Series Game 6 in 1997 drew a baseball record 67,498.

parks.name: Cleveland Hardware Field
parks.status: Housing now covers the site; coordinates are the city center.
notable: At East 79th Street and Kinsman Road.
Used by the 1931 Cubs and the 1932 Cleveland Stars.
Home of the Cleveland Bears in 1939 and 1940.

parks.name: Harlan Field
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Listed as the 1925 home of the Wilmington Potomacs.

parks.name: Harrison Park
parks.status: A luxury apartment building and a Montessori school stand on the site.
notable: Federal League Newark Peppers played here in 1915; the opener drew 26,032.
Only one Federal League home run cleared the fence here.

parks.name: Hartford Ball Club Grounds
parks.status: A lawn across from the Church of the Good Shepherd; a plaque once marked the site.
notable: Home of the Hartford Dark Blues from 1874 to 1876.
A 2008 memorial plaque was stolen in 2009 and recovered in 2017.
Home of the Hartford Dark Blues from 1874 through 1876, two seasons in the NA and one in the NL.

parks.name: Haymakers' Grounds
parks.status: Near Knickerbacker Park, where a monument marks Troy's brief major league history.
notable: Home of the Troy Haymakers in 1871 and 1872, and later of the Troy Trojans in 1880-81.
A 1992 monument ceremony included an exhibition game played by 1882 rules.
Also called the Vail Lot after an early settler family.

parks.name: Hilldale Park
parks.status: Retail stores and parking lots; a Pennsylvania historical marker stands there.
notable: Home of the Hilldale Club from 1910 to 1932.
A tree in center field was treated as in play.
Site of the 1925 Negro League World Series games.

parks.name: Hilltop Park
parks.status: Demolished; NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia medical center stands there and a plaque marks home plate.
notable: Home of the Highlanders for 1903 through 1912, on the heights of Washington Heights.
Jack Chesbro's wild pitch there on the last day cost the Highlanders the 1904 pennant.
The Giants borrowed it in 1911 after a fire destroyed the Polo Grounds.

parks.name: Hinchliffe Stadium
parks.status: Reopened in 2023 after renovation; a National Historic Landmark hosting minor-league baseball and soccer.
notable: Main home of the New York Cubans in 1935-36 and the Black Yankees in 1937-38.
Designated a National Historic Landmark in 2013.

parks.name: Howard Avenue Grounds
parks.status: Sold to developers by 1888; residences now cover the lot.
notable: Normal home field of the New Haven Elm Citys in their 1875 season.
Hartford hosted an 1877 National League game here.

parks.name: Hubert H. Humphrey Metrodome
parks.status: Demolished in 2014. U.S. Bank Stadium now stands on the site.
notable: Twins won the 1987 and 1991 World Series here.
Its fabric roof collapsed under snow in December 2010.
Hosted a Super Bowl, an All-Star Game and Final Fours.

parks.name: Huntington Avenue Grounds
aka: Huntington Avenue American League Baseball Grounds
parks.status: Demolished in 1912; Northeastern University's Cabot Center stands on the site.
notable: Hosted the first modern World Series game in 1903.
Cy Young pitched the first modern perfect game there on May 5, 1904.
Built on a former circus lot; a tool shed stood in play in deep center.

parks.name: Home grounds not recorded
parks.status: No fixed home park is recorded for this traveling or poorly documented club.
notable: Club played without a documented home ballpark.
Coordinates are the city center.

parks.name: International Fair Association Grounds
parks.status: Site is now residential streets in the Hamlin Park neighborhood.
notable: Home of the Buffalo Federal League club in 1914-15.
Built on part of a former fairgrounds with horse and bicycle tracks.

parks.name: Island Park
parks.status: On City Island; ballfield later reused for baseball.
notable: Home of the Harrisburg Giants from 1922 to 1927.
The Giants also played Sundays at Rossmere Park in Lancaster.
Home of the 1943 Harrisburg-St. Louis Stars of the Negro National League.

parks.name: Jarry Park Stadium
parks.status: Converted to a tennis venue, now Stade IGA, inside Jarry Park.
notable: Hosted the first MLB regular-season game in Canada on April 14, 1969.
Bill Stoneman threw the first big-league no-hitter outside the US here in 1972.
Willie Stargell once drove a ball into the pool beyond right field.

parks.name: Jefferson Street Grounds
parks.status: A public school, recreation center and ball fields now occupy the site.
notable: Hosted the National League's first game on April 22, 1876, a 6-5 Boston win over Athletic.
Toledo's Moses Fleetwood Walker caught here in a May 1884 game against the Athletics.
Served as the Athletics' home for all of 1883-1890 before their AA expulsion.

parks.name: Kennard Street Park
parks.status: Commercial buildings now cover the site near East 46th Street and Carnegie Avenue.
notable: Home of the Cleveland Blues throughout their NL run, 1879-84.
Later renamed National League Park; Cleveland's second NL Park was a few blocks northwest.

parks.name: Keystone Park
parks.status: Former baseball ground on the old Forepaugh circus lot; no ballpark remains.
notable: Home of the Philadelphia Keystones in 1884.
Sources disagree on whether it lay east or west of South Broad Street.

parks.name: Kingdome
parks.status: Imploded in 2000; Lumen Field now stands on the site.
notable: Imploded in 2000, a record for the largest building demolished that way.
Hosted Edgar Martinez's walk-off double in the 1995 ALDS.

parks.name: Lakefront Park
parks.status: Site lies within Millennium Park; the ballpark is long gone.
notable: Rebuilt on the old Lake Park site; the club hit 142 home runs here in 1884 after the fence became home run territory.
Right field was very short, under 200 feet, which fed the 1884 home run surge.

parks.name: League Park
parks.status: Site is now a public park; the restored ticket house holds a baseball museum.
notable: Game 5 of the 1920 World Series had the first Series grand slam and an unassisted triple play.
Babe Ruth hit his 500th home run here in 1929.
Short right-field line was backed by a 40-foot wall.

parks.name: League Park (Cincinnati)
parks.status: Palace of the Fans replaced it on the same block; the site no longer has a ballpark.
notable: Opening day 1884 saw a grandstand collapse that killed one spectator.
Center field fence painted black in 1895, sometimes called the first batter's eye.

parks.name: League Park
parks.status: Not recorded in sources checked; it lay a few blocks northwest of Fifth Third Field.
notable: Home of the 1884 Toledo Blue Stockings, who featured Moses Fleetwood Walker.
Stood on a block bounded by Monroe, 15th, Jefferson and 13th.

parks.name: Lloyd Street Grounds
parks.status: Demolished in 1904; the site is now a residential neighborhood.
notable: Home of the 1901 Milwaukee Brewers, the American League's first Milwaukee club, who finished last.
Home plate sat near Lloyd Street, so the field faced due north.
The Brewers' first major league game there was played on May 3, 1901.

parks.name: Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum
parks.status: The Coliseum still stands, used for USC football and slated for the 2028 Olympics.
notable: A 42-foot screen guarded the 251-foot left-field line, producing cheap home runs.
Game 5 of the 1959 World Series drew 92,706 fans.
Dodgers played here 1958-61 before Dodger Stadium opened.

parks.name: Louisville Baseball Park
parks.status: The block became the St. James Court residential neighborhood.
notable: Home of the Louisville Grays in 1876 and 1877, the club's only two seasons.
The same block later held the Southern Exposition from 1883 to 1887.

parks.name: Luna Park
parks.status: Housing now covers the site; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Ballpark inside an amusement park.
Home of the 1928 Cleveland Tigers.
Home of the 1933 Cleveland Giants of the Negro National League.

parks.name: Mack Park
parks.status: Demolished in the 1960s; Fairview Homes senior housing now stands on the site.
notable: Detroit Stars home from 1920 through 1929.
A 1929 fire, started while drying the field with gasoline, destroyed the grandstand.
Built by semipro sponsor Joe Roesink at Mack and Fairview Avenues.

parks.name: Madison Avenue Grounds
parks.status: Eutaw Street now cuts through the former grounds in West Baltimore.
notable: Baltimore's first enclosed ballpark, built by the Waverly Club.
Cincinnati beat the local Marylands 47-7 there in 1869.

parks.name: Mansfield Club Grounds
parks.status: A residential development now occupies the hilltop site.
notable: Named for Civil War general Joseph K. Mansfield, as was the team.
Brickworks owner Dewitt Clinton Sage donated the land in 1871.

parks.name: Martin Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1961; a semi-truck dealership stands there with a historical marker.
notable: Built in 1923 by R. S. Lewis as Lewis Park for the Red Sox.
Renamed for the Martin brothers after their 1927 purchase.
Expanded in 1947 at a cost of $200,000.

parks.name: Maryland Baseball Park
parks.status: Site of the Wheelabrator Baltimore plant.
notable: Home of the Baltimore Black Sox in the 1920s.
Stood about half a mile north of Westport Park.

parks.name: Meadowbrook Oval
parks.status: Site on South Orange Avenue is now West Side High School.
notable: Listed as the home of the Newark Dodgers in 1934-35.
Opening year not found; value shown is first known Negro-league use. Other sources name Sprague or Ollemar fields.

parks.name: Memorial Stadium
parks.status: Demolished starting in 2001; a youth sports field and senior apartments stand there.
notable: Home of the Orioles for 1954 through 1991, and the Colts and Ravens in football.
A small plane crashed into the upper deck after a December 1976 playoff game.
Inner fences added after 1958 shrank the deep outfield dimensions.

parks.name: Messer Street Grounds
parks.status: Demolished in 1887; houses were built on the land.
notable: Providence installed the first professional backstop here in 1878.
Fans could watch from a building roof beyond the left field fence for 25 cents.

parks.name: Metropolitan Park
parks.status: 1199 Plaza, a residential complex, stands on the site.
notable: Built on landfill in East Harlem; players and writers nicknamed it The Dump.
The Metropolitans opened here May 13, 1884, then moved back to the Polo Grounds.
The Mets won 26 of 33 home games here in 1884.

parks.name: Metropolitan Park
parks.status: Site near North Broadway and Clarence Avenue is now an industrial area.
notable: Formerly Giants Park II; home of the St. Louis Giants in 1920-21.
Home of the 1937 St. Louis Stars of the Negro American League.

parks.name: Metropolitan Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1985. The Mall of America stands on the site.
notable: Hosted the 1965 All-Star Game and World Series.
Harmon Killebrew hit a 520-foot homer here in 1967.
Also hosted the Vikings, including the 1969 NFL title game.

parks.name: Home grounds not recorded
parks.status: No fixed home park is recorded for this traveling or poorly documented club.
notable: Club played without a documented home ballpark.
Coordinates are the city center.

parks.name: Mile High Stadium
parks.status: The site is a parking lot for the Broncos' stadium, marked by a home plate plaque.
notable: Rockies set MLB attendance records here in 1993.
Movable east stands slid on water bearings to switch between football and baseball.
Built on a former landfill.

parks.name: Milwaukee County Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 2001. Parking for American Family Field and Helfaer Field cover the site.
notable: First American ballpark built with public funds.
Hank Aaron hit his 755th and final home run here in 1976.
Hosted the 1957 and 1958 World Series and two All-Star Games.

parks.name: Municipal Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1976. A garden and housing redevelopment occupy the site.
notable: Royals played here 1969 to 1972 before moving to Kauffman Stadium.
Hosted the longest NFL game ever, a 1971 Dolphins-Chiefs playoff.
Opened in 1923 as Muehlebach Field.

parks.name: National Association Grounds
parks.status: Site at Central Avenue and East 55th Street; current use not documented in source.
notable: Home of the Cleveland Forest Citys in 1871 and 1872, who won five of sixteen home games.
Hosted a short-lived Forest City club in the 1912 United States Baseball League.

parks.name: National League Park II
parks.status: Not recorded in sources checked; the area is now commercial.
notable: Called Association Park in 1887-88 and National League Park in 1889-90.
Bounded by Payne, Euclid, East 30th and East 40th (Case) Avenues.
Replaced by League Park for the Spiders in 1891.

parks.name: Neil Park
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the Columbus Buckeyes in their 1921 NNL season.
Retrosheet lists 1921 NNL games here.

parks.name: Home grounds not recorded
parks.status: No fixed home park is recorded for this traveling or poorly documented club.
notable: Club played without a documented home ballpark.
Coordinates are the city center.

parks.name: Newell Park
parks.status: Former ballfield at East Raynor Street and South Salina Street; present use not stated.
notable: Home of the 1879 Syracuse Stars, who folded on September 10 with a 22-48 record.
Historians also call it Star Park I.

parks.name: Newington Park
parks.status: Replaced by houses and a church.
notable: Home of the National Association's Lord Baltimore club from 1872 to 1874.
Hosted the Baltimore Orioles' first American Association season, 1882.
Baltimore Canaries played here from 1872 to 1874, and the Orioles used it until 1882.

parks.name: Oakdale Park
parks.status: Torn down shortly after 1883; the site was redeveloped.
notable: Philadelphia Athletics played 39 home games here in the American Association's first season, 1882.
The club left for Jefferson Street Grounds in 1883.

parks.name: Oakland Coliseum
parks.status: Still standing; used for soccer, cricket and events after the Athletics left.
notable: Catfish Hunter and Dallas Braden each threw a perfect game here.
Last U.S. stadium shared by baseball and football teams.

parks.name: Olympic Park (Buffalo)
parks.status: A residential area including the Richmond-Summer Recreation Center occupies the site.
notable: Home of the NL Bisons in 1884 and 1885, then International League clubs through 1888.
Built on the former Riverside Park site; its stands were later moved to a second Olympic Park.
Leased by the Players' League Buffalo Bisons in 1890.

parks.name: Olympic Stadium
parks.status: Still stands as an events venue; a new roof is under construction.
notable: Built for the 1976 Olympics; the Expos moved in for 1977.
Hosted the 1982 All-Star Game before 59,057 fans.
The retractable roof was replaced by a fixed one in 1998.

parks.name: Olympics Grounds
parks.status: Block between 16th and 17th Streets NW at S Street, now mixed residential and commercial.
notable: Named for the Olympic club; home to Washington's National Association clubs from 1871 to 1875.
The club's earlier home, the White Lot, was also called Olympic Grounds.

parks.name: Oriole Park I
parks.status: Closed after 1888; later Oriole Parks stood on nearby blocks.
notable: First of several Baltimore ballparks named Oriole Park, used by the Orioles from 1883 to 1888.
Sat near present-day East 25th and Barclay Streets.

parks.name: Oriole Park II
parks.status: Closed in 1891 when the Orioles moved to Union Park.
notable: Home of the Orioles from 1889 until early May 1891.
Located at Greenmount Avenue and East 29th Street in Waverly.

parks.name: American League Park (Baltimore)
parks.status: Gone; a McDonald's and row houses stand near the site.
notable: Opened April 26, 1901, with the Orioles beating Boston 10-6 behind Joe McGinnity.
Located at Greenmount Avenue and 29th Street; the minor-league Orioles used the site afterward.
Final 1902 home game drew only 138 paid fans.

parks.name: Palace of the Fans
parks.status: Demolished after 1911 and replaced by Redland Field on the same site.
notable: Ornate facade with 22 Corinthian columns; fans could drive carriages to stalls beneath the grandstand.
Among the earliest parks built largely of concrete.

parks.name: Parkway Field
parks.status: Site is an intramural field near the University of Louisville; the diamond is gone.
notable: Home of the Louisville Black Caps from 1930 to 1932.
Used by Louisville Colonels from 1923 into the 1950s.
Center field ran about 512 feet in 1936.

parks.name: Passon Field
parks.status: Site at 48th and Spruce Streets is now a West Philadelphia High School football field.
notable: Home of the Philadelphia Bacharach Giants about 1932-34 and the Stars in 1934-35.
Opening year not found; value shown is the first known Negro-league use.

parks.name: Pencoyd Field
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are near Wissahickon station.
notable: Home of the 1928 Philadelphia Tigers in Manayunk.

parks.name: Perry Park
parks.status: Park is closed; present use of the site is not documented in sources.
notable: Used only in 1875, when the Keokuk Westerns went 1-12.
Westerns played their first home game there on May 4, 1875, against Chicago.

parks.name: Polo Grounds
parks.status: Demolished in 1964; the Polo Grounds Towers public housing complex stands on the site.
notable: Yankees tenants from 1913 through 1922, then Giants and 1962-63 Mets.
Horseshoe shape and a 483-foot center field earned it a bathtub nickname.
Site of Bobby Thomson's 1951 pennant-winning home run.

parks.name: Polo Grounds (I)
parks.status: Streets and buildings north of Central Park cover the site after demolition in 1889.
notable: Stood at 110th-112th Streets north of Central Park.
Home to the Gothams and Giants 1883-88 and the Metropolitans.
Torn down in 1889 when 111th Street was cut through.

parks.name: Polo Grounds (II)
parks.status: Site paved over as a parking lot in 1948; structures were razed earlier.
notable: Located at 155th Street and Eighth Avenue beside Coogan's Hollow.
Giants called it home 1889-90 while the Players' League used the neighboring park.
Later used by the Manhattan Athletic Club.

parks.name: Ponce de Leon Park
parks.status: A strip mall stood here, later demolished; the magnolia tree remains.
notable: A center-field magnolia kept balls in play until the wall moved in 1947.
Atlanta Black Crackers shared the park with the white Crackers.
Hosted Atlanta's first integrated crowd in 1962.

parks.name: Putnam Grounds (Troy)
parks.status: Exact site not recorded in sources consulted; city-center coordinates used.
notable: Treated as the home of the 1879 Troy Trojans in their first NL season.
Troy moved to the Haymakers' Grounds for 1880.

parks.name: Recreation Park (Detroit)
parks.status: Harper Hospital buildings stand on the site, with a historical marker in former left field.
notable: Hosted Detroit's first major league game on May 2, 1881.
The Wolverines won the 1887 NL pennant and World Series here.

parks.name: Recreation Park I
parks.status: Interstate 70 ramps now cover the site.
notable: Home of the Columbus Buckeyes in 1883 and 1884.
The 1884 Buckeyes went 69-39 here.

parks.name: Recreation Park II
parks.status: A vacant store lot and houses occupy the Schumacher Place site.
notable: Home of the Columbus Solons in 1889-1891.
Ohio State played its first home football game here on November 1, 1890.
A historical marker for that game was placed on the site in 2006.

parks.name: Recreation Park
parks.status: Demolished around 1890. Urban housing and a corner mini market occupy the site.
notable: Phillies played their first home game here on May 1, 1883.
Charlie Ferguson threw the club's first no-hitter here in 1885.
Served as a horse market in the late 1870s before baseball.

parks.name: Recreation Park (Pittsburgh)
parks.status: Industrial buildings covered the site starting in the early 1900s.
notable: Hosted the Alleghenys' first officially recognized NL game, a 6-2 win over Chicago on April 30, 1887.
Also the site of an 1892 football game with a paid player, Pudge Heffelfinger.

parks.name: Red Bird Stadium
parks.status: Later Cooper Stadium; closed in 2008 and left half-demolished and abandoned by 2021.
notable: Home of the 1933 Columbus Blue Birds and the 1935 Columbus Elite Giants.
Built from the same blueprints as Red Wing Stadium in Rochester.

parks.name: Red Stocking Park
parks.status: A transit agency repair facility occupies the site beneath the Compton Avenue viaduct.
notable: Home of the 1875 St. Louis Red Stockings, who quit mid-season.
Six people were arrested for cutting holes in the fence to watch games.

parks.name: Red Wing Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1997-98; an industrial and office park now occupies the site.
notable: Site of the New York Black Yankees' final 1948 season.
Renamed Silver Stadium in 1968.

parks.name: Rickwood Field
parks.status: Still standing as a preserved working ballpark and museum that hosts an annual game.
notable: Oldest surviving professional ballpark in the United States.
Shared by the Birmingham Black Barons and the white Birmingham Barons.
Called the oldest surviving professional ballpark in the United States.

parks.name: Ridgewood Park
parks.status: Replaced by industrial buildings in 1959.
notable: Brooklyn used this Queens ground mainly for Sunday games to dodge Brooklyn's blue laws.
The Brooklyn Gladiators played their whole 1890 home schedule here.
The grandstand burned on September 19, 1917.

parks.name: Riverfront Stadium
parks.status: Imploded in 2002; Great American Ball Park and other developments now occupy the site.
notable: First stadium to use AstroTurf across the whole field except the bases and mound.
Hosted the 1970 and 1988 All-Star Games.

parks.name: Riverside Park
parks.status: Part of the residential Prospect Hill neighborhood.
notable: First ballpark of the major league Bisons, used 1879-83.
Named for the river but sat several blocks from it; demolished by its owner for redevelopment.

parks.name: Robert F. Kennedy Memorial Stadium
parks.status: Demolished through 2025-2026. Sports fields and a skate park occupy the campus.
notable: Early dual-purpose cookie-cutter stadium for baseball and football.
The Senators' last game here in 1971 ended in a forfeit.
Nationals played here from 2005 through 2007.

parks.name: Robison Field
parks.status: Beaumont High School was built on the site in 1926 and closed in 2014.
notable: Last major league ballpark built mainly of wood; fires burned the grandstand in 1898 and 1901.
Renamed Robison Field in 1911 for the former club owners Frank and Stanley Robison.

parks.name: Ruppert Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1967; a food products plant now occupies the site.
notable: Home of the Newark Eagles from 1936 to 1948, shared with the Newark Bears of the International League.
Opened as Davids' Stadium, later Bears Stadium, before taking the Ruppert name in 1932.
Opened as Davids' Stadium; the Newark Stars played here in 1926.

parks.name: Sahlen Field
parks.status: Still in use as the home of the Triple-A Buffalo Bisons.
notable: Blue Jays' temporary home for the 2020 season and part of 2021.
Opened in 1988 as the first modern retro-style ballpark.
Blue Jays played their first game there on August 11, 2020.

parks.name: San Diego Stadium
parks.status: Demolished by 2021; SDSU's Snapdragon Stadium and campus expansion now occupy the site.
notable: Hosted the World Series in 1984 and 1998.
Tony Gwynn's final game was played here in 2001.
Was the first octorad stadium, a square-circle design.

parks.name: Seals Stadium
parks.status: A shopping center now occupies the Mission District site.
notable: Hosted the first West Coast major-league game, April 15, 1958.
Home of the Pacific Coast League Seals before the Giants arrived.
Giants used it 1958-59 while Candlestick Park was built.

parks.name: Shea Stadium
parks.status: Demolished after 2008; part of the Citi Field parking lot covers the site.
notable: Yankees shared it with the Mets in 1974 and 1975 during Yankee Stadium's renovation.
The Mets won the 1969 and 1986 World Series there.
The Beatles drew a record 55,600 fans in 1965.

parks.name: Shibe Park
parks.status: Demolished in 1976. A church sanctuary now occupies the site.
notable: Baseball's first steel-and-concrete stadium.
Hosted the first AL night game in 1939.
Renamed Connie Mack Stadium in 1953; Phillies played here 1938 to 1970.

parks.name: Sick's Stadium
parks.status: A Lowe's store now stands on the site, with markers showing the old diamond.
notable: Home of the Seattle Pilots in their lone 1969 season; seating, plumbing and upkeep problems plagued it.
Named for brewery owner Emil Sick; it replaced Dugdale Field, destroyed by arson in 1932.

parks.name: South End Grounds
parks.status: Demolished. Northeastern University science complex and Ruggles station area occupy the site.
notable: Rebuilt after the 1894 Roxbury fire destroyed the second park.
Cy Young made his last Boston home start here in 1911.
Short lines and deep center gave it almost no real left or right field.

parks.name: South End Park
parks.status: Location and current use not found.
notable: Home of the St. Louis Stars in 1939 and the St. Louis half of 1941.
Opening year not found; value shown is first known use.

parks.name: South Side Park
parks.status: Burned in 1940 and demolished. Wentworth Gardens public housing now occupies the site.
notable: White Sox home from 1901 until June 1910; the Sox won the 1906 World Series here.
Hosted the Chicago American Giants and the 1913 Negro league postseason series.
Burned in December 1940 and was not rebuilt.

parks.name: South Side Park (I)
parks.status: Block at 39th and Wabash left as disused ground after 1884; no ballpark remains.
notable: Built in 1883; the Chicago Browns played 35 home games there in 1884.
A misfired fireworks shell at a July 1884 show killed a woman nearby.
No photographs or drawings are known.

parks.name: South Side Park (II)
parks.status: Footprint became the Comiskey Park site; the south end is now a parking lot.
notable: Called Brotherhood Park in 1890, when the Chicago Pirates played here.
The NL Chicago club used it in 1891-93 before moving to West Side Park.
Used by the NL club for a partial 1891 schedule and the full 1892 season; Sunday ball was barred by its lease.

parks.name: South Street Park
parks.status: A parking lot for Gainbridge Fieldhouse covers the block.
notable: Home of the 1878 Indianapolis Blues, a one-season National League club.
Hosted some Chicago White Stockings games in 1878 as a neutral site.

parks.name: Speranza Park
parks.status: Not recorded in sources checked.
notable: Reportedly named after the club owner's yacht; speranza means hope in Italian.
The Maumees played their first home game May 1, 1890 and finished a few games over .500.

parks.name: Sportsman's Park
parks.status: Demolished in 1966; a Boys & Girls Club stands on the site.
notable: Shared by the Browns and Cardinals, who both played there from 1920 until the Browns left after 1953.
Hosted the 1926 World Series and All-Star Games in 1940, 1948 and 1957.
Renamed Busch Stadium in 1953 after the Cardinals' owner bought it.

parks.name: St. George Cricket Grounds
parks.status: The Empire Outlets shopping center stands on the site.
notable: Home of the Metropolitans in 1886-87, nicknamed Mutrie's Dump after manager Jim Mutrie.
The Giants played here in spring 1889 while the Polo Grounds was closed.
Fans could see the Statue of Liberty under construction.

parks.name: Star Park II
parks.status: The city later ran South Clinton Street through the property.
notable: Home of the 1890 Syracuse Stars of the American Association.
Stood in the block between Salina, Taylor, Oneida and Temple Streets, crossed by a railroad track.

parks.name: Stars Park
parks.status: Site is now the Harris-Stowe State University baseball field with a Stars Park monument.
notable: Built in 1922 for the St. Louis Stars, one of few parks built for a Negro league club.
Hosted games of the 1925, 1928, and 1930 NNL championship series.
A photograph of the park surfaced only in 2016.

parks.name: Swampoodle Grounds
parks.status: Part of the area was absorbed into Union Station and the old Main Post Office.
notable: Named for the Swampoodle neighborhood; fans could see the Capitol dome from the stands.
Home of the Washington Nationals for their four NL seasons, 1886-89.

parks.name: Swayne Field
parks.status: Shopping center now stands; part of the left-field wall remains.
notable: Home of the Toledo Mud Hens from 1909 to 1955.
Toledo Tigers played their 1923 NNL season here.
Named for donor Noah Swayne Jr.

parks.name: Tate Field
parks.status: Now a golf course; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the Tate Stars in 1922 and later the Browns, Elites, and Hornets.
Renamed Hooper Field; Beyerle and Sykora Roads bounded it.

parks.name: TD Ballpark
parks.status: Still in use as the Blue Jays' spring training home.
notable: Blue Jays hosted 21 regular-season home games here in April and May 2021.
Spring home of the Blue Jays since their first season in 1977.
A $102 million renovation reopened it in February 2020.

parks.name: Terrapin Park
parks.status: Destroyed by fire in July 1944.
notable: Built for the Federal League Baltimore Terrapins in 1914; later called Oriole Park (V).
A 1944 fire destroyed the mostly wooden park.

parks.name: Three Rivers Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 2001; the site is mostly parking with offices and commemorative markers.
parks.architect: Deeter Ritchey Sipple; Michael Baker Jr.
notable: Hosted the first night game in World Series history, Game 4 in 1971.
Also the site of the Immaculate Reception in 1972.

parks.name: Tiger Stadium
parks.status: Demolished 2008-09. The field was preserved as the Corner Ballpark youth field.
notable: Babe Ruth hit a 1921 homer estimated at up to 575 feet.
Lou Gehrig ended his 2,130-game streak here in 1939.
Hosted the 1941, 1951 and 1971 All-Star Games.

parks.name: Tinker Park
parks.status: Methodist Hospital of Indianapolis now occupies the site.
notable: Also called Seventh Street Park and Athletic Park; the 1884 Indianapolis club played here.
Blue laws pushed Sunday games to suburban grounds in later years.
Butler's football team hosted three games here in 1887.

parks.name: Tom Wilson Park
parks.status: Demolished; the source does not say what occupies the site now.
notable: Built by owner Thomas T. Wilson for the Nashville Elite Giants.
Stood in Trimble Bottom, then Nashville's largest Black community.
Built by owner Tom Wilson for the Nashville Elite Giants.

parks.name: Troy Ball Clubs Grounds
parks.status: Vacant fields on 1903 maps; the later use of the site is not recorded in sources consulted.
notable: Built in 1882 for $5,000 on a former wheat field in West Troy.
Home of the Troy Trojans' final NL season; later minor league clubs used it into the 1890s.

parks.name: Turner Field
parks.status: Reconfigured as Center Parc Stadium, a Georgia State University football venue.
parks.architect: Heery, Rosser, Williams-Russell and Johnson, Ellerbe Becket
notable: Built as the Olympic stadium for 1996, then converted to baseball.
Hosted the 2000 All-Star Game and the first NL Wild Card Game in 2012.
Record crowd of 54,357 came on October 5, 2003.

parks.name: Union Base-Ball Grounds
parks.status: Site lies within Millennium Park, in the area now called Wrigley Square.
notable: Home of the Chicago White Stockings in 1871 before the Great Chicago Fire destroyed it.
The club lost its equipment and records in the fire and did not play in 1872-73.

parks.name: Union Grounds
aka: Union Base Ball and Cricket Grounds
parks.status: Streets, a secondary school and an armory now cover the Williamsburg site.
notable: First baseball park fully enclosed by a fence, which let the owner charge admission.
Had a pagoda in center field and was flooded for ice skating in winter.
Last major league game there was July 26, 1878, Providence over Milwaukee.

parks.name: Union Grounds
parks.status: Cleared in 2019 for a federal geospatial intelligence agency facility.
notable: Home of the St. Louis Maroons in the Union Association (1884) and National League (1885-86).
Henry Lucas created both the league and the club.
Stands were demolished in 1888.

parks.name: Union Park
parks.status: The site is now a residential neighborhood in Barclay.
notable: Opened May 11, 1891 with an 8-4 Orioles win over the St. Louis Browns.
Dan Brouthers's 1894 homer reportedly rolled onto 23rd Street, later joked to be a 1,300-foot shot.
A January 1895 fire burned the grandstand, which was rebuilt.

parks.name: Union Street Park
parks.status: Former park site at Union and Front (now Lancaster Avenue) streets.
notable: Home of the Wilmington Quicksteps in their 18-game Union Association run.
The Quicksteps drew only about 400 fans per game.

parks.name: Veterans Stadium
parks.status: Imploded in 2004. A parking lot with commemorative markers sits on the site.
notable: Phillies won their first World Series here in 1980.
Hosted baseball's latest finish, a 4:40 a.m. end in 1993.
AstroTurf earned it the Field of Seams nickname.

parks.name: Washington Park (I)
parks.status: The reconstructed Old Stone House, once part of the park, stands in Washington Park, Brooklyn.
notable: Hosted ice baseball games in 1884.
The Old Stone House sheltered team equipment during the May 1889 fire.
Nearby streetcar lines inspired the Trolley Dodgers nickname.

parks.name: Washington Park (II)
parks.status: Part of the left-center wall survives inside a Con Edison yard on Third Avenue.
notable: Opened April 30, 1898 before about 15,000 fans.
Rebuilt in steel and concrete in 1914 by the Federal League Tip-Tops.
Fumes from the nearby Gowanus Canal gave it a famous odor.

parks.name: Washington Park
parks.status: Mostly covered by the Indianapolis Zoo; a marker was placed in 2011.
notable: Home of the Indianapolis ABCs from 1920 to 1926.
Enlarged to about 20,000 seats after a 1909 rebuild.
Said to be the largest field in the minor leagues.

parks.name: Home grounds not recorded
parks.status: No fixed home park is recorded for this traveling or poorly documented club.
notable: Club played without a documented home ballpark.
Coordinates are the city center.

parks.name: Waverly Fairgrounds
parks.status: Site is now split between Weequahic Park in Newark and a cemetery in Elizabeth.
notable: Elizabeth Resolutes lost all seven of their home National Association games here in 1873.
Hosted the New Jersey State Fair from 1867 to 1898.

parks.name: West Seventh Street Park
parks.status: Former ballpark site on West Seventh Street; exact location not confirmed.
notable: Nominal home of the Union Association St. Paul club, which played no home games.
Also called Fort Street or Fort Road Grounds.

parks.name: West Side Grounds
parks.status: Torn down in 1920; the University of Illinois Medical Center occupies the site.
notable: Cubs won the 1907 and 1908 World Series here, their last titles until 2016.
Hosted the 1906 World Series, the first Series between two teams from the same city.

parks.name: West Side Park
parks.status: Site is now occupied by Chicago World Language Academy on West Harrison Street.
notable: Mostly wooden park that opened June 6, 1885; the club left after the 1891 season.
Right field distance is disputed in sources, reported between 216 and 225 feet.

parks.name: Westwood Field
parks.status: Site not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the Dayton Marcos in 1920 and 1926.
Opened as West Side Park; Marcos opened their 1920 NNL home slate here.

parks.name: Worcester Driving Park Grounds
parks.status: Streets, homes and businesses cover it; a granite post marks the perfect game on the old Becker campus.
notable: Lee Richmond threw the first major league perfect game here on June 12, 1880.
On September 25, 1882, one admission covered two games against Providence.

parks.name: Wright Street Grounds
parks.status: Former ballpark site; current use not confirmed.
notable: Filled a city block bounded by Wright, Clarke, 11th and 12th Streets.
The Union Association Brewers played here from September 27 to October 12, 1884.

parks.name: Wrigley Field
parks.status: Demolished; a mental health center, parking and a Little League field occupy the site.
notable: The 1961 Angels hit a record 248 home runs here.
Hosted the first NFL Pro Bowl in 1939.

parks.name: Yankee Stadium (1923)
parks.status: Demolished 2009-2010; Heritage Field public park now occupies the site.
notable: Opened April 18, 1923, with Babe Ruth hitting the first home run.
Host of Don Larsen's 1956 World Series perfect game.
Renovated in 1974-75; the Yankees played at Shea Stadium in the interim.
